name: Scholar's Mate
about: The most famous beginner trap: White's queen and bishop both attack f7, and if Black doesn't notice, it is checkmate on move four. Every player must know it, mostly so it never happens to you.
ideas: The queen and the bishop both aim at f7.
f7 is weak because only the king protects it.
Black stops it easily with ...g6 or ...Qe7, then gains time attacking White's queen.
short: A 4-move checkmate trick with the queen and bishop.
starts: White brings the queen to h5 and the bishop to c4, both aiming at f7.
why: Learn it so it never happens to you.
named: Called 'scholar's' because it catches new players who are still learning.

lines.name: The trap
notes: White opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
Black develops but doesn't see the danger.
The queen comes out early and also aims at f7. Now Qxf7 is checkmate if nothing is done.
A big mistake. The knight attacks the queen, but it doesn't protect f7.
Checkmate! The queen takes on f7, the bishop protects her, and the king can't escape.

lines.name: How Black stops it: ...g6
notes: White opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
Black develops but doesn't see the danger.
The queen comes out early and also aims at f7. Now Qxf7 is checkmate if nothing is done.
Black blocks the queen's line to f7 and attacks the queen.
The queen goes back and aims at f7 again.
The knight now blocks the queen's line to f7. Black is safe.
Black develops. White's queen came out too early and Black is doing well.

lines.name: How Black stops it: ...Qe7
notes: White opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
Black develops but doesn't see the danger.
The queen comes out early and also aims at f7. Now Qxf7 is checkmate if nothing is done.
The queen protects f7 and the e5 pawn at the same time.
Now the knight attacks White's queen and Black gains time.
The queen has to move again. Lesson: bringing the queen out early wastes moves.

lines.name: Early queen: 2.Qh5
notes: White opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
The queen comes out on move two and attacks e5 and f7.
The bishop joins the attack on f7.
Black blocks the queen and attacks her.
The queen goes back to aim at f7.
The knight blocks f7. Black is safe and better developed.

name: Fool's Mate
about: The fastest checkmate in chess: just two moves. It only happens if White moves the f-pawn and the g-pawn early, which opens the diagonal to White's king. The lesson: don't weaken the pawns in front of your king.
ideas: Moving the f-pawn and g-pawn early opens a road to your king.
The queen on h4 gives check along that diagonal.
Nothing can block the check, so it is mate.
short: The fastest checkmate in chess: 2 moves.
starts: White moves the f-pawn and g-pawn, and Black's queen jumps to h4.
why: Shows why you must not open the pawns in front of your king.
named: Only a 'fool' would let it happen.

lines.name: Two-move checkmate
notes: A weak first move: it opens the e1-h4 diagonal to White's king.
Black opens a path for the queen.
Another weak move. Now there is nothing between h4 and White's king.
Checkmate! The queen checks along the diagonal and nothing can block or capture her.

lines.name: Same idea after 1.f4
notes: This pawn move also opens the diagonal to White's king.
Black opens a path for the queen.
Checkmate again. Keep the f-pawn and g-pawn at home in the opening.

name: Légal's Mate
about: A famous trap from the 1700s. White seems to give away the queen, but if Black takes it, White's minor pieces give checkmate. It teaches that a pin is not always real.
ideas: The bishop on g4 pins the f3 knight to White's queen.
White breaks the pin anyway because there is a mate.
Lesson: before you grab the queen, check for checks.
short: A trick where White gives away the queen and still wins.
starts: Black pins White's knight, White ignores the pin and lets Black take the queen.
why: Teaches you to look for checks before grabbing a piece.
named: Named after Monsieur de Légal, a French player from the 1700s.

lines.name: The trap
notes: Black protects e5 with a pawn (Philidor Defense).
Black pins the f3 knight to White's queen.
A slow move. Black doesn't notice the danger on f7.
Surprise! The knight takes, leaving the queen to be taken.
Black grabs the queen. This loses.
The only move for the king.
Checkmate with three minor pieces. The queen was a bait.

lines.name: Black doesn't take the queen
notes: Black protects e5 with a pawn (Philidor Defense).
Black pins the f3 knight to White's queen.
A slow move. Black doesn't notice the danger on f7.
Surprise! The knight takes, leaving the queen to be taken.
White wins the bishop back and is a pawn up. Black still lost material, but no mate.

name: Blackburne Shilling Trap
about: A trick for Black in the Italian Game. Black moves the knight to d4 and leaves e5 unprotected. If White greedily takes on e5, Black's queen attacks and the game ends in mate.
ideas: ...Nd4 looks like a mistake but sets a trap.
Greedy Nxe5 lets Black's queen attack g2 and f2.
If White doesn't take, the trick is not very good, so use it carefully.
short: A trap for Black in the Italian Game.
starts: Black moves a knight to d4 and leaves a pawn as bait.
why: A fun trick to know, and to avoid as White.
named: Joseph Blackburne, a famous English player, is said to have won a shilling (a coin) a game with it.

lines.name: The trap
notes: The Italian bishop aims at f7.
The trap: Black leaves e5 without protection.
The queen attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2.
White also attacks the queen and the rook. It looks great for White.
Black's queen attacks the h1 rook.
Checkmate! A knight check that the king can't escape.

lines.name: The right answer for White
notes: The Italian bishop aims at f7.
The trap: Black leaves e5 without protection.
White swaps knights instead of taking e5.
White opens lines and will win the d4 pawn or get a better centre.

name: Englund Gambit Trap
about: A trap for Black against 1.d4. Black offers a pawn, and if White plays a natural-looking bishop move, Black's queen runs into White's position and gives checkmate on c1.
ideas: Black gives a pawn to get fast attacking chances.
...Qb4+ attacks the king and the b2 pawn together.
Against a good player this gambit is risky for Black.
short: A trap for Black when White starts with the queen's pawn.
starts: Black gives a pawn with ...e5 and sets a queen trick.
why: Good to know as White so you don't fall for it.
named: Named after Fritz Englund, a Swedish player.

lines.name: The trap
notes: The Englund Gambit: Black offers a pawn.
The queen attacks e5 again and prepares the trick.
A natural move that protects e5, but it falls into the trap.
Check, and the queen also attacks b2.
The queen takes b2 and attacks the a1 rook.
Black pins the bishop to the king.
Checkmate! The queen takes over the first row.

lines.name: The right answer for White
notes: The Englund Gambit: Black offers a pawn.
The queen attacks e5 again and prepares the trick.
The queen protects e5 and attacks f7. White keeps the extra pawn and is better.

name: Italian Game
about: One of the oldest openings, played for more than 400 years. White brings the bishop to c4, where it aims at f7, the weakest square near Black's king. It is a great first opening: you develop fast, castle early and learn the main ideas of open games.
ideas: Put pawns in the centre, then bring out knights and bishops.
The bishop on c4 looks at f7, the square only the king protects.
Castle early, then slowly prepare d4 to take more of the centre.
short: Best first opening: pawn to the centre, knight out, bishop to c4.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. White's bishop looks at Black's weak f7 square.
why: Play it as White. Simple ideas, quick castling.
named: Italian players wrote about it in the 1500s.

lines.name: Giuoco Piano, quiet main line
notes: White takes the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop.
Black does the same: a pawn in the centre, so White's pawn can't push on.
The knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5. Developing with a threat is always good.
Black defends e5 with a knight and develops at the same time.
The Italian bishop. It points at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Black copies the idea: this bishop points at f2, White's weak square.
White prepares d4. With a pawn on c3, White can push d4 and recapture with a pawn.
Black develops and attacks the e4 pawn, so White has to look after it.
A calm way to protect e4. White builds a solid centre first and plays d4 later.
Black also protects e5 and opens a path for the other bishop.
White castles. The king is safe in the corner and the rook is ready to join the game.
Black castles too. Both kings are safe, so now the middle game starts.
The rook moves to e1 to support the e4 pawn and a later d4 push.
Black makes room for the bishop: if White plays b4 or d4, the bishop can drop back to a7.
White moves the bishop away from ...b5 or ...d5 attacks. It still aims at f7 from b3.

lines.name: Two Knights Defense
notes: White takes the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop.
Black does the same: a pawn in the centre, so White's pawn can't push on.
The knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5. Developing with a threat is always good.
Black defends e5 with a knight and develops at the same time.
The Italian bishop. It points at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Instead of ...Bc5, Black attacks e4 at once. This is sharper and more active.
White attacks f7 a second time: knight and bishop both hit it.
Black blocks the bishop's line to f7 by pushing a pawn in front of it.
White takes the pawn. Now Black must be careful.
The best answer: the knight attacks the c4 bishop. Taking back on d5 with the knight would allow a dangerous attack (see the Fried Liver).
White saves the bishop with check.
Black blocks the check and attacks the d5 pawn and the bishop.
White takes, so Black is now a pawn down.
Black takes back. Black gave up a pawn but has quick development and open lines.
The bishop goes back to safety.
Black kicks the g5 knight. In return for the pawn, Black's pieces will be very active.

lines.name: Fried Liver Attack (a trap to know)
notes: White takes the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop.
Black does the same: a pawn in the centre, so White's pawn can't push on.
The knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5. Developing with a threat is always good.
Black defends e5 with a knight and develops at the same time.
The Italian bishop. It points at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Black blocks the bishop's line to f7.
A mistake that looks natural. Now f7 is very weak again.
White gives up the knight to drag the king out.
Black takes, and the king has to come forward.
Check, and the queen also attacks the d5 knight, which is pinned to the king.
The king has to protect the knight himself. A king in the middle of the board is in great danger.
White adds another attacker on d5. Lesson: after Ng5, answer with ...Na5, not ...Nxd5.

lines.name: Evans Gambit
notes: White takes the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop.
Black does the same: a pawn in the centre, so White's pawn can't push on.
The knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5. Developing with a threat is always good.
Black defends e5 with a knight and develops at the same time.
The Italian bishop. It points at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Black copies the idea: this bishop points at f2, White's weak square.
White offers a pawn to win time: if Black takes, White plays c3 and d4 with gain of tempo.
White attacks the bishop and prepares d4.
The bishop steps back but still pins along the a5-e1 diagonal.
White grabs the centre. Black's pieces must react.
White castles and gets ready to attack. White is a pawn down but much faster.

name: Ruy Lopez (Spanish Game)
about: Named after a Spanish priest from the 1500s, this is a favourite of world champions. White's bishop goes to b5 and attacks the knight that defends e5. White plays for small long-lasting pressure rather than a quick attack.
ideas: Bb5 puts pressure on the knight that guards e5.
White aims for c3 and d4, a big centre.
Black often plays ...a6 and ...b5 to push the bishop back.
short: White's bishop goes to b5 and slowly pushes Black around.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. Like the Italian, but the bishop goes one square further.
why: Play it as White once the Italian feels easy.
named: Named after Ruy López, a Spanish priest who wrote about it in 1561.

lines.name: Closed main line
notes: The Spanish bishop attacks the knight that is defending e5.
Black asks the bishop: are you going to take my knight or move back?
White keeps the bishop and the pressure. Taking on c6 is the Exchange Variation.
White castles. If Black takes on e4, White can win it back with Re1.
Black develops calmly and prepares to castle.
Black pushes the bishop away from the pin.
The bishop is now on a good diagonal, aiming at f7.
Black protects e5 and frees the c8 bishop.
White prepares the d4 push and gives the bishop a retreat square on c2.
A useful little move: it stops ...Bg4 pinning the f3 knight. Now White can play d4.

lines.name: Berlin Defense
notes: The Spanish bishop attacks the knight that is defending e5.
Black ignores the bishop and attacks e4 straight away.
White castles and lets the pawn go for now.
White opens the centre to use the faster development.
The knight hits the b5 bishop.
Black takes back, opening the d-file for the queen.
White wins back the pawn and attacks the d6 knight.
Queens come off. This endgame is very solid for Black and is called the Berlin Wall.
Black can't castle any more, but with queens gone the king is safe enough.

lines.name: Exchange Variation
notes: The Spanish bishop attacks the knight that is defending e5.
Black asks the bishop: are you going to take my knight or move back?
White gives the bishop for the knight to damage Black's pawns.
Black takes towards the centre and opens lines for the queen and bishop.
White castles. Now Nxe5 would be a real threat.
Black protects e5 with a pawn.
White takes back. In the endgame White hopes the extra pawn on the king side will count.
Black chases the knight away and gets space.

name: Scotch Game
about: White opens the centre straight away with d4 on move three. The game becomes open, with fast development and clear plans. Garry Kasparov made it popular again in the 1990s.
ideas: d4 opens the centre early and frees White's pieces.
White's knight on d4 is strong in the middle of the board.
Black must develop quickly and attack the d4 knight.
short: White opens the centre straight away with d4.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4. Pawns swap in the middle and the game opens up.
why: Play it as White if you like open, fast games.
named: Named after a match played by Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1824.

lines.name: Classical Variation
notes: The Scotch: White attacks e5 again and opens the centre.
Black takes. Keeping the pawn on e5 is not possible.
White takes back with the knight, which stands strongly in the middle.
Black develops and attacks the d4 knight.
White defends the knight with the bishop.
Black adds a third attacker on d4.
White protects d4 with a pawn, so the knight is now very safe.
Black develops, keeping the f-pawn free and the queen's line open.
White develops the last minor piece and points at f7.

lines.name: Schmidt Variation (4...Nf6)
notes: The Scotch: White attacks e5 again and opens the centre.
Black takes. Keeping the pawn on e5 is not possible.
White takes back with the knight, which stands strongly in the middle.
Black pins the e5 pawn to the king.
The knight jumps to a strong central square.
White kicks the knight again and gains space.

lines.name: Scotch Gambit
notes: The Scotch: White attacks e5 again and opens the centre.
Black takes. Keeping the pawn on e5 is not possible.
Instead of taking back, White develops and lets the pawn go for a while.
White pushes and attacks the knight.
Black hits the c4 bishop. This is the right way to meet White's attack.
The bishop steps aside and pins the c6 knight.
The knight finds a strong square in the centre.

name: Four Knights Game
about: Both sides bring out all four knights first. It is calm, logical and very good for beginners: you follow the rule 'knights before bishops' and keep the position safe.
ideas: Knights come out first, towards the centre.
Both sides castle quickly.
Watch for pins with Bb5 and Bg5.
short: Both sides bring out all four knights first.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6. Four knights, two each side.
why: Very simple and safe. Great for beginners as White.
named: The name just counts the knights.

lines.name: Spanish Variation
notes: White protects e4 and develops the second knight.
Black does the same. All four knights are out.
The bishop pins the c6 knight a little and adds pressure on e5.
White protects e4 and opens the c1 bishop.
White pins the f6 knight to the queen.

lines.name: Scotch Four Knights
notes: White protects e4 and develops the second knight.
Black does the same. All four knights are out.
White takes back with the knight.
Black pins the c3 knight, so e4 is weaker.
Black takes back with a nice centre pawn.
Black castles. An equal, open game.

lines.name: Rubinstein Variation
notes: White protects e4 and develops the second knight.
Black does the same. All four knights are out.
The bishop pins the c6 knight a little and adds pressure on e5.
Black doesn't copy White: the knight jumps forward and offers a pawn.
Black develops fast and aims at f2.
Black castles and gets very quick, active play for the pawn.

name: Vienna Game
about: White plays Nc3 on move two and keeps the f-pawn free. Later White can push f4, like a King's Gambit but better prepared. It leads to lively games.
ideas: Nc3 protects e4 and keeps the f-pawn free.
The push f4 attacks Black's centre.
White often aims for an attack on the king side.
short: White guards e4 with a knight and later pushes the f-pawn.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3. Then often f4 to attack Black's centre.
why: Play it as White if you like attacking.
named: Popular with players in Vienna, Austria, in the 1800s.

lines.name: Vienna Gambit
notes: The Vienna: the knight guards e4 and stays out of the f-pawn's way.
The Vienna Gambit: White attacks e5 with a pawn.
The best answer: Black hits back in the centre.
Black takes the e4 pawn with a strong knight.
Black develops and gets ready to castle.
Black castles. Both sides have a good game.

lines.name: Quiet line with Bc4
notes: The Vienna: the knight guards e4 and stays out of the f-pawn's way.
Black develops the queen side knight.
Now White pushes f4 with good support.
White develops. White hopes for an attack after f4-f5.

name: King's Gambit
about: White offers the f-pawn on move two to pull Black's e-pawn away and open the f-file. It was the most popular opening in the 1800s and leads to wild attacking games.
ideas: f4 offers a pawn to take control of the centre.
The f-file opens for White's rook.
White's own king can become weak, so play fast.
short: White gives a pawn on move 2 to attack fast.
starts: 1.e4 e5 2.f4. White offers the f-pawn to open lines.
why: Exciting, but risky. For players who love attacks.
named: 'Gambit' means giving something away to get an advantage.

lines.name: Accepted, Kieseritzky
notes: The King's Gambit: White offers a pawn.
The knight stops ...Qh4+ and prepares d4.
Black protects the extra pawn on f4.
Black pushes forward and attacks the knight.
The knight jumps to a strong central square.
The knight drops back and attacks f4.
White wins back a pawn. The game is open and sharp.

lines.name: Declined, Classical
notes: The King's Gambit: White offers a pawn.
Black says no thanks. The bishop on c5 stops White from castling short.
White pushes and attacks the bishop.
White takes back with a big centre.
The bishop gives check and stays active.

lines.name: Accepted, Modern Defense
notes: The King's Gambit: White offers a pawn.
The knight stops ...Qh4+ and prepares d4.
Black gives the pawn back to free the game.
Black develops and gets ready to castle. A balanced game.

name: Queen's Gambit
about: White offers the c-pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away from the centre. It is not a real gamble: White can almost always win the pawn back. One of the most solid and respected openings in chess.
ideas: c4 attacks d5 so White can take over the centre.
If Black takes on c4, White wins the pawn back later.
Pressure on the d5 square and the pin Bg5 are key ideas.
short: White starts with the queen's pawn and offers another pawn.
starts: 1.d4 d5 2.c4. White offers the c-pawn to pull Black's pawn away from the centre.
why: Play it as White if you start with 1.d4. Very solid.
named: 'Gambit' means offering something; here White usually wins the pawn back.

lines.name: Declined, Orthodox
notes: White takes the centre with the queen's pawn.
Black stops White's pawn from going further.
The Queen's Gambit: White offers a pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away.
Black declines. The e6 pawn protects d5 firmly.
White pins the f6 knight, so it can't help d5 as freely.
White protects d4 and opens the f1 bishop.
Black develops and keeps c-pawn free for ...c6 or ...c5.
The rook goes to the c-file, which will open soon.
Now Black takes, because White has spent a move with the bishop.
Black swaps some pieces to get more room. A classic plan.

lines.name: Exchange Variation
notes: White takes the centre with the queen's pawn.
Black stops White's pawn from going further.
The Queen's Gambit: White offers a pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away.
Black declines. The e6 pawn protects d5 firmly.
White swaps pawns in the centre.
Black takes back. Black's c8 bishop now has an open diagonal.
Black protects d5 and keeps a strong pawn chain.
White prepares long-term plans, like a pawn push b4-b5 to attack Black's queen side.

lines.name: Accepted
notes: White takes the centre with the queen's pawn.
Black stops White's pawn from going further.
The Queen's Gambit: White offers a pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away.
Black takes the pawn, but does not try to keep it.
White opens the bishop to win the c4 pawn back.
Black prepares ...b5 to gain space on the queen side.

lines.name: Slav Defense
notes: White takes the centre with the queen's pawn.
Black stops White's pawn from going further.
The Queen's Gambit: White offers a pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away.
The Slav: Black protects d5 with the c-pawn and keeps the c8 bishop free.
White stops ...b5, which would keep the extra pawn.
The bishop comes out before ...e6 locks it in. That is the point of the Slav.
White prepares to win back c4.
Black castles. A solid, equal position.

name: London System
about: A system: White sets up the same pieces almost every game, whatever Black does. Pawns on d4, e3 and c3 and a bishop on f4. Easy to learn, very solid, and popular at every level.
ideas: The bishop comes to f4 before e3, so it is not locked in.
Pawns on c3, d4 and e3 make a strong triangle.
White often attacks later with Ne5 and a king side push.
short: White sets up the same pieces almost every game.
starts: 1.d4 and 2.Bf4, then pawns on e3 and c3.
why: Easy to learn because the plan hardly changes.
named: Named after a tournament in London in 1922.

lines.name: Main setup
notes: The London bishop comes out first, before e3 can block it.
White protects d4 and opens the f1 bishop.
White protects d4 with a pawn: the London triangle c3-d4-e3.
Black adds more pressure on d4.
The knight goes to d2, not c3, because the c-pawn is already on c3.
Black offers to swap the strong f4 bishop.
White develops the last piece and aims at Black's king.

lines.name: Against a King's Indian setup
notes: Black wants to put the bishop on g7.
The bishop on the long diagonal.
The bishop goes to e2, safe from ...Nh5 or ...e5 ideas.
A safety move: the bishop on f4 can retreat to h2.

name: English Opening
about: White starts with the c-pawn. It controls d5 from the side instead of taking the centre straight away. The game is often slower and more about clever piece play.
ideas: c4 controls d5 from the flank.
White often puts the bishop on g2 to aim along the long diagonal.
It can turn into many other openings, so it is flexible.
short: White starts with the c-pawn instead of the centre pawns.
starts: 1.c4. White controls the centre from the side.
why: For calm players who like slow, clever games.
named: An English player, Howard Staunton, used it in 1843.

lines.name: Reversed Sicilian
notes: The English: White controls d5 from the side.
White prepares to put the bishop on g2.
Black takes space in the centre.
Black takes back with the knight.
The bishop now hits the d5 knight along the long diagonal.

lines.name: Symmetrical Variation
notes: The English: White controls d5 from the side.
White prepares the bishop on g2.
Both bishops look at the long diagonal.
Black castles. A slow, equal game.

name: Sicilian Defense
about: The most popular answer to 1.e4. Black fights for d4 with the c-pawn instead of copying White. The position becomes unbalanced, so Black plays for a win, not just a draw.
ideas: ...c5 controls d4 from the side.
After d4 and ...cxd4, Black has an extra centre pawn.
Black often attacks on the queen side while White attacks the king.
short: Black answers 1.e4 with the c-pawn and plays to win.
starts: 1.e4 c5. Black doesn't copy White and fights from the side.
why: Play it as Black against 1.e4 if you like sharp fights.
named: Written about by an Italian from Sicily in the 1600s.

lines.name: Najdorf Variation
notes: The Sicilian: Black attacks d4 from the side.
Black controls e5 and opens the c8 bishop.
Black swaps a side pawn for a centre pawn.
White takes back with the knight.
The Najdorf. This stops Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares ...e5 or ...b5.
White develops, planning f3, Qd2 and castling long.
Black kicks the d4 knight and takes space.
Black develops and gets ready to castle.

lines.name: Dragon Variation
notes: The Sicilian: Black attacks d4 from the side.
Black controls e5 and opens the c8 bishop.
Black swaps a side pawn for a centre pawn.
White takes back with the knight.
The Dragon: the bishop will go to g7. The pawn shape looks like a dragon.
The Dragon bishop on the long diagonal.
White protects e4 and plans Qd2 and castling long.
The bishop aims at f7 and Black's king. Both sides race to attack.

lines.name: Alapin Variation (2.c3)
notes: The Sicilian: Black attacks d4 from the side.
White prepares d4 with a pawn, so Black can't remove the centre.
White pushes and kicks the knight.
The knight jumps to a strong square.
White takes back with a pawn.

lines.name: Closed Sicilian (2.Nc3)
notes: The Sicilian: Black attacks d4 from the side.
White keeps the centre closed and plays slowly.
White prepares the bishop on g2.
White plans an attack on the king side with f4-f5.

name: French Defense
about: Black plays ...e6 and then ...d5 to challenge White's centre. It is solid and strategic. The c8 bishop is sometimes locked in, so Black often counterattacks with ...c5 and ...f6.
ideas: ...e6 and ...d5 attack White's e4 pawn.
Black hits the d4 pawn with ...c5.
The light-squared bishop on c8 is Black's problem piece.
short: Black answers 1.e4 with ...e6, then hits back with ...d5.
starts: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. A strong wall of pawns for Black.
why: Play it as Black against 1.e4 if you like solid positions.
named: French players used it in a match against London in 1834.

lines.name: Classical, Steinitz
notes: White pushes and kicks the knight.
Black attacks the base of White's pawn chain.
White takes back with the knight.
Black attacks the knight and develops.

lines.name: Advance Variation
notes: White pushes at once and gains space.
Black attacks the d4 pawn, the base of White's chain.
The queen also hits d4 and b2.
White prepares b4 to gain space.
Black locks the queen side to stop b4.

lines.name: Exchange Variation
notes: Black takes back. The c8 bishop is free now.
Black castles. A calm, equal game.

lines.name: Winawer Variation
notes: The Winawer: Black pins the c3 knight, which protects e4.
White asks the bishop to decide.
Black takes the knight, damaging White's pawns.
White takes back. White has doubled pawns but two strong bishops.
